quotes.t: My meaning simply is, that whatever I have tried to do in life, I have tried with all my heart to do well.
It was one of those March days when the sun shines hot and the wind blows cold: when it is summer in the light, and winter in the shade.
There is a passion for hunting something deeply implanted in the human breast.
It is a melancholy truth that even great men have their poor relations.
Beauty is not caused. It is.
Dying is a wild night and a new road.
The truth must dazzle gradually, or every man be blind.
A wounded deer leaps highest.
An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.
He that lieth down with dogs, shall rise up with fleas.
He that is of the opinion money will do everything may well be suspected of doing everything for money.
Fish and visitors stink in three days.
No, no, we are not satisfied, and we will not be satisfied until justice rolls down like waters and righteousness like a mighty stream.
Let us not wallow in the valley of despair.
This is no time to engage in the luxury of cooling off or to take the tranquilizing drug of gradualism.
I cannot fix on the hour, or the spot, or the look, or the words, which laid the foundation. It is too long ago. I was in the middle before I knew that I had begun.
In vain I have struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.
There is a stubbornness about me that never can bear to be frightened at the will of others. My courage always rises at every attempt to intimidate me.
I have learnt that all men live not by care for themselves but by love.
He who has love, is in God, and God is in him, for God is love.
It is not beauty that endears, it's love that makes us see beauty.
As long as this exists, this sunshine and this cloudless sky, and as long as I can enjoy it, how can I be sad?
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl (23 February 1944)

quotes.t: I think it's odd that grown-ups quarrel so easily and so often and about such petty matters. Up to now I always thought bickering was just something children did and that they outgrew it.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl (28 September 1942)

quotes.t: Everyone has inside of him a piece of good news. The good news is that you don't know how great you can be! How much you can love! What you can accomplish! And what your potential is!
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl

quotes.t: Enemies are always friends waiting to be made.
There is no point in exacting vengeance. It never satisfies the hunger it sets out to appease.
Resentment and anger are bad for your blood pressure and your digestion.
Something is always born of excess: great art was born of great terrors, great loneliness, great inhibitions, instabilities, and it always balances them.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anais Nin, Vol. 4: 1944-1947

quotes.t: Our life is composed greatly from dreams, from the unconscious, and they must be brought into connection with action. They must be woven together.
I could be healed by the sheer courage of continuing to live. I could heal myself.
quotes.source: A Journal of Love: The Unexpurgated Diary of Anais Nin, 1931-1932

quotes.t: No man is happy who does not think himself so.
quotes.source: The Moral Sayings of Publius Syrus (Maxim 584)

quotes.t: The judge is condemned, when the criminal is acquitted.
quotes.source: The Moral Sayings of Publius Syrus (Maxim 407)

quotes.t: It is a universal law which ordains birth and death.
quotes.source: The Moral Sayings of Publius Syrus (Maxim 421)

quotes.t: Man is a tool-using animal. Without tools he is nothing, with tools he is all.
The true university of these days is a collection of books.
quotes.source: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841), The Hero as Man of Letters

quotes.t: All that mankind has done, thought, gained or been: it is lying as in magic preservation in the pages of books.
quotes.source: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841), The Hero as Man of Letters

quotes.t: Examine for a moment an ordinary mind on an ordinary day.
Second-hand books are wild books, homeless books; they have come together in vast flocks of variegated feather, and have a charm which the domesticated volumes of the library lack.
The past only comes back when the present runs so smoothly that it is like the sliding surface of a deep river.
I had worked hard for nearly two years, for the sole purpose of infusing life into an inanimate body.
A new species would bless me as its creator and source; many happy and excellent natures would owe their being to me.
The fallen angel becomes a malignant devil. Yet even that enemy of God and man had friends and associates in his desolation; I am alone.
The setting sun will always set me to rights, or if a sparrow come before my window, I take part in its existence and pick about the gravel.
The excellence of every art is its intensity, capable of making all disagreeables evaporate, from their being in close relationship with Beauty and Truth.
quotes.source: Letter to George and Tom Keats, 21 December 1817

quotes.t: The only means of strengthening one's intellect is to make up one's mind about nothing — to let the mind be a thoroughfare for all thoughts, not a select party.
quotes.source: Letter to George and Georgiana Keats, September 1819

quotes.t: It's really hard to design products by focus groups. A lot of times, people don't know what they want until you show it to them.
I didn't see it then, but it turned out that getting fired from Apple was the best thing that could have ever happened to me.
The heaviness of being successful was replaced by the lightness of being a beginner again, less sure about everything.
However good a Constitution may be, it is sure to turn out bad because those who are called to work it, happen to be a bad lot.
Caste has killed public spirit. Caste has destroyed the sense of public charity. Caste has made public opinion impossible.

If we wish to maintain democracy not merely in form, but also in fact, what must we do? The first thing in my judgement we must do is to hold fast to constitutional methods of achieving our social and economic objectives.
You can only be afraid of what you think you know.
Thought is so cunning, so clever, that it distorts everything for its own convenience.
All outward forms of change brought about by wars, revolutions, reformations, laws and ideologies have failed completely to change the basic nature of man and therefore of society.
Do your work with your whole heart, and you will succeed — there's so little competition.
The world is moving so fast these days that the man who says it can't be done is generally interrupted by someone doing it.
The line between failure and success is so fine that we scarcely know when we pass it — so fine that we are often on the line and do not know it.
He who receives an idea from me, receives instruction himself without lessening mine; as he who lights his taper at mine, receives light without darkening me.
The earth belongs always to the living generation.
Determine never to be idle. No person will have occasion to complain of the want of time who never loses any. It is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing.
Would you not like to try all sorts of lives — one is so very small — but that is the satisfaction of writing — one can impersonate so many people.
We are tardy in believing, when belief brings hurt.
No mockery in this world ever sounds to me so hollow as that of being told to cultivate happiness.
Those who profess to favor freedom and yet deprecate agitation are men who want crops without plowing up the ground.
I exist as I am, that is enough.
True law is right reason in agreement with nature.
It is the end of a family — when they begin to sell their land. Out of the land we came and into we must go — and if you will hold your land you can live — no one can rob you of land.
Whatever you fight, you strengthen, and what you resist, persists.
One must not put a loaded rifle on the stage if no one is thinking of firing it.
It is impossible to build one's own happiness on the unhappiness of others.
Champions aren't made in gyms. Champions are made from something they have deep inside them — a desire, a dream, a vision.
The foundation stones of honesty, character, faith, integrity, love, and loyalty are necessary for a balanced success that includes health, wealth, and happiness.
Death closes all: but something ere the end, some work of noble note, may yet be done.
The three great essentials to achieve anything worthwhile are, first, hard work; second, stick-to-itiveness; third, common sense.
Happiness is not something you postpone for the future; it is something you design for the present.
quotes.source: The Treasury of Quotes by Jim Rohn

quotes.t: In science, we should be interested in things, not persons.
After all, you only find out who is swimming naked when the tide goes out.

Living is like tearing through a museum. Not until later do you really start absorbing what you saw, thinking about it, looking it up in a book, and remembering — because you can't take it all in at once.
We all want to help one another. Human beings are like that. We want to live by each other's happiness — not by each other's misery.
You can make more friends in two months by becoming genuinely interested in other people than you can in two years by trying to get other people interested in you.
quotes.source: How to Win Friends and Influence People

quotes.t: If a man will begin with certainties, he shall end in doubts; but if he will be content to begin with doubts, he shall end in certainties.
Great works are performed, not by strength, but by perseverance.
Sometimes your best investments are the ones you don't make.
Learn to labor and to wait.
Know then thyself, presume not God to scan; the proper study of mankind is man.
I was born a slave, but nature gave me the soul of a free man.
For hatred is corrosive of a person's wisdom and conscience; the mentality of enmity can poison a nation's spirit.
quotes.source: I Have No Enemies: My Final Statement (2009)

quotes.t: A true man should take full responsibility for his own actions.
Life resembles a novel more often than novels resemble life.
The universe may one day perish, yet my vows are eternal.
Do good deeds, speak good words, think good thoughts.
I want to sleep a while, a while, a minute, a century; but let everyone know that I have not died.
O Chinese, why aren't you angry?
A letter from home is worth ten thousand in gold.
A person's perfection is measured not by the information or knowledge they possess, but by the depth of their charity.
When those red berries come in springtime, flushing on your southland branches, take home an armful, for my sake, as a symbol of our love.
In heaven, may we be birds flying wing to wing; on earth, may we be branches grown together.
Long I lived checked by the bars of a cage; now I have turned again to Nature and Freedom.
Love is not reason; love is not common sense.
Heaven and earth have a spirit of integrity; in many forms does it flow into all things.

Alexander Pope.bio: English poet and master of the heroic couplet. His works include An Essay on Criticism, The Rape of the Lock and An Essay on Man, along with celebrated translations of Homer.

Alfred Tennyson.bio: English Poet Laureate; author of In Memoriam and Ulysses.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Anton Chekhov.bio: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright and master of the short story, a practising doctor who wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya and hundreds of stories. His restrained, humane art reshaped both the theatre and short fiction of the 20th century.

Audrey Hepburn.bio: Audrey Hepburn was a British actress and humanitarian celebrated for films such as Roman Holiday, Breakfast at Tiffany's and My Fair Lady. In later life she devoted herself to UNICEF, serving as a Goodwill Ambassador in some of the world's poorest regions.

B.R. Ambedkar.bio: Indian jurist and social reformer who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and campaigned against caste discrimination.

Bai Juyi.bio: Bai Juyi was a Tang-dynasty Chinese poet famous for verse so plainspoken that, legend says, he read each poem to an old washerwoman and rewrote whatever she could not understand. His 'Song of Everlasting Regret' remains beloved across East Asia.

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Charles Reade.bio: Charles Reade was an English novelist and dramatist whose The Cloister and the Hearth is a richly researched tale of 15th-century Europe. A meticulous collector of facts and documents, he campaigned through his fiction against abuses in prisons and asylums.

Charlie Chaplin.bio: Charlie Chaplin was an English comic actor and filmmaker whose Little Tramp became a global icon of silent cinema. He co-founded United Artists and wrote, directed and starred in classics including City Lights, Modern Times and The Great Dictator.

Charlotte Brontë.bio: English novelist, author of Jane Eyre.
Charlotte Brontë.credit: Alonzo Chappel, Public domain (File: File:Charlotte Bronte by Alonzo Chappel.jpg)

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

Daisaku Ikeda.bio: Daisaku Ikeda was a Japanese Buddhist philosopher, educator and peace activist who led the Soka Gakkai lay Buddhist movement and founded Soka University. He wrote extensively on Buddhism, dialogue and peace.

Dale Carnegie.bio: Dale Carnegie was an American writer and lecturer on self-improvement and public speaking. His book How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936) became one of the best-selling books of all time.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Donald Trump.bio: Donald Trump is an American businessman and television personality who served as the 45th President of the United States (2017–2021) and was elected again as the 47th President in 2024. Before politics he built a real-estate business and hosted the reality show The Apprentice.

Du Fu.bio: Du Fu is regarded as China's greatest poet, a Tang-dynasty writer whose work earned him the title 'Poet-Sage'. Writing through war and political collapse, he fused personal hardship with deep compassion for ordinary people.

Eckhart Tolle.bio: Eckhart Tolle is a German-born spiritual teacher living in Canada, author of The Power of Now (1997) and A New Earth (2005), books on presence and the ego that became international bestsellers.

Elbert Hubbard.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, publisher and philosopher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community. His essay "A Message to Garcia" (1899) was one of the most widely reprinted works of its era; he died in the sinking of the Lusitania.

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Federico García Lorca.bio: Federico García Lorca was a Spanish poet and playwright, author of the Gypsy Ballads and the tragedies Blood Wedding and The House of Bernarda Alba. He was murdered by Nationalist forces at the start of the Spanish Civil War, at thirty-eight.

Francis Bacon.bio: Francis Bacon was an English philosopher, statesman and essayist who championed the empirical method of inquiry. His Essays and his plan for the reform of learning in the Novum Organum helped lay the groundwork of modern science.

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

George Sand.bio: George Sand, the pen name of Amandine Dupin, was a French novelist and journalist who scandalised and fascinated 19th-century Paris. Her novels of love and rural life, and her independent personal life, made her one of the most notable women writers of her century.

Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.bio: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was an American poet and educator, among the most popular poets of his century. He wrote Paul Revere's Ride, The Song of Hiawatha and Evangeline, and produced the first American translation of Dante's Divine Comedy.

Hsing Yun.bio: Hsing Yun was a Chinese Buddhist monk who founded the Fo Guang Shan monastery and the Buddha's Light International Association in Taiwan. He promoted 'Humanistic Buddhism' and his 'four givings': confidence, joy, hope, and convenience to others.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jiddu Krishnamurti.bio: Indian philosopher and speaker on the nature of mind, meditation, and human freedom; rejected all guru roles.

Jim Rohn.bio: Emanuel James Rohn, known as Jim Rohn, was an American entrepreneur and motivational speaker whose seminars and books on personal development influenced a generation of speakers, including Tony Robbins.

Jin Yong.bio: Jin Yong was a Hong Kong novelist whose wuxia martial-arts epics, such as The Legend of the Condor Heroes, have been read by hundreds of millions across the Chinese-speaking world. He also co-founded the newspaper Ming Pao.

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

Katherine Mansfield.bio: New Zealand modernist short-story writer, a leading figure of early 20th-century literature alongside Joyce and Woolf.
Katherine Mansfield.credit: Archives New Zealand from New Zealand, CC BY-SA 2.0

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Liu Xiaobo.bio: Liu Xiaobo was a Chinese literary critic, writer, and human-rights activist who co-authored the Charter 08 manifesto. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2010 while imprisoned, and his final statement was titled 'I Have No Enemies'.

Lung Ying-tai.bio: Lung Ying-tai is a Taiwanese writer and essayist, and served as Taiwan's first Minister of Culture. Her book of essays on family, Mu Song ('Watching You Go'), moved readers across the Chinese-speaking world.

Marie Curie.bio: Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who pioneered the study of radioactivity, a term she coined. She remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911 — and died of illness caused by her long exposure to radiation.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Muhammad Ali.bio: American heavyweight boxing champion and cultural icon known as much for his activism as his titles.

Ovid.bio: Ovid was a Roman poet celebrated for the Metamorphoses, a vast narrative poem of mythological transformations. Exiled by the emperor Augustus to the Black Sea coast, he spent his last decade writing poems of lament and endurance.

Pearl Buck.bio: Pearl S. Buck was an American writer who spent much of her early life in China, where her parents were missionaries. Her novel The Good Earth won the Pulitzer Prize, and she received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Samuel Johnson.bio: Samuel Johnson was an English writer who compiled the first great Dictionary of the English Language in 1755. Poet, essayist and the most quoted conversationalist of his age, his life was immortalised in Boswell's famous biography.

Sheng Yen.bio: Sheng Yen was a Taiwanese Chan (Zen) Buddhist master and scholar who founded Dharma Drum Mountain. He popularized a practical way through difficulty: face it, accept it, deal with it, then let it go.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Tao Yuanming.bio: Tao Yuanming was a Chinese poet who gave up a government career to farm and write in the countryside. His 'Peach Blossom Spring' and drinking poems made him the patron saint of the simple, self-chosen life.

Teresa of Ávila.bio: Teresa of Ávila was a Spanish Carmelite nun, mystic and reformer of the Carmelite order. Her spiritual classics The Interior Castle and The Way of Perfection, written with disarming directness, made her one of the most influential women writers of early modern Europe.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Thomas Edison.bio: Thomas Edison was an American inventor who developed the phonograph, the motion picture camera and the first practical electric light bulb. He held over a thousand US patents and founded the first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey.

Thomas Jefferson.bio: Thomas Jefferson was an American statesman and Founding Father who wrote the Declaration of Independence and served as the third President of the United States (1801–1809). He founded the University of Virginia and doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase.

Toussaint Louverture.bio: Formerly enslaved leader of the Haitian Revolution who defeated French, Spanish and British forces and abolished slavery in Saint-Domingue. His generalship and statecraft laid the ground for Haiti, the first free Black republic.

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).

Wang Wei.bio: Wang Wei was a Tang-dynasty Chinese poet, painter, and Buddhist known for serene landscape poetry. Poems such as 'Deer Enclosure' distill a whole mountainside into a few quiet lines.

Warren Buffett.bio: Investor Warren Buffett, the 'Oracle of Omaha', turned Berkshire Hathaway into one of the world's largest conglomerates through patient, disciplined value investing. Famous for his annual shareholder letters and frugal personal habits, he has pledged to give away the great majority of his fortune.

Wen Tianxiang.bio: Wen Tianxiang was a Song-dynasty scholar-official and poet who refused to serve the Mongol conquerors and was executed after years in prison. His 'Song of Righteousness' and his prison poems made him a lasting symbol of loyalty.

Zig Ziglar.bio: Zig Ziglar was an American author and motivational speaker who became one of the most influential sales and personal-development trainers of the twentieth century. His book See You at the Top and his famous line 'Your attitude, not your aptitude, will determine your altitude' reached millions.
